about: The deep zoom's generated pictures (the owner's ask, Sat 31 Oct 2026: improve the images at the extremes of the scale, above Studio 45 and below the atom, with pictures made by Antigravity from written prompts, in place of the diagrams). draw.py sends each prompt to `agy -p` (Antigravity's image-generator subagent, model pro); make_webp.py puts each on the page's night sky and writes docs/reports/ladder-img/<file>. Each picture is an illustration, not a photograph or a measurement: the drawings' numbers, seats and scale bars stay the page's own, and README.md records where each scene places its picture.
credit: an AI illustration made for this page with Google Antigravity (a Gemini image model) from a written prompt: not a photograph or a measurement

style.space: Photorealistic astronomical illustration in the manner of NASA/JPL-Caltech and ESO artist's concepts, high detail, physically plausible colours. Pure black background (#000000) everywhere outside the subject, fading smoothly to pure black at all four edges. No text, no letters, no labels, no captions, no arrows, no grid, no border, no frame, no watermark, no signature.
style.particle: Scientific illustration of particle physics, physically motivated, cinematic and softly glowing, shallow depth of field. Pure black background (#000000) everywhere outside the subject, fading smoothly to pure black at all four edges. No text, no letters, no symbols, no labels, no arrows, no border, no frame, no watermark, no signature.

images.prompt: A square 1:1 image. An imagined view from outside our observable universe. At the exact centre of the frame, our universe as a softly glowing translucent sphere whose diameter is 30% of the image width, filled with a faint web of luminous blue-white filaments and edged with a thin warm orange rim. Around it, scattered across a dark void at different distances and depths, nine other faint translucent bubbles of different sizes (from 8% to 26% of the image width) and slightly different tints (pale blue, violet, pale gold), the farther ones dimmer and smaller, none touching the central sphere, as if other regions or universes might exist. Very sparse faint dust between them. Speculative, dreamlike but photographic.

A square 1:1 image. The observable universe drawn as a sphere seen from outside, centred exactly in the frame, its diameter 88% of the image width. Inside the sphere, the cosmic web in three dimensions: glowing blue-white filaments made of countless tiny galaxies, meeting at bright knots (galaxy clusters) and separated by large dark empty voids, denser and finer toward the centre. At the sphere's surface, a thin translucent shell of mottled warm orange and red light (the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light), brightest along the limb, with a subtle speckled texture. A single tiny bright point at the very centre. Pure black outside the sphere.

A square 1:1 image. A three-dimensional visualization of the Laniakea supercluster of galaxies seen from outside, centred in the frame and filling about 90% of it, in the spirit of Tully, Courtois, Hoffman and Pomarede's 2014 Nature visualization. An irregular, lobed cloud made of countless tiny glowing points (galaxies), concentrated along thin filaments and in a few dense knots, coloured from deep blue in sparse regions through cyan to white and pale gold in the densest. Thin white flow lines (the streamlines of the galaxies' motions) run inward from all around the cloud's edge and converge on one dense bright knot just right of and below the centre (the Great Attractor). Pure black around the cloud.

A square 1:1 image. The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) at the exact centre of the frame: a large spiral galaxy tilted about 77 degrees from face-on, so it appears as a long ellipse whose long axis runs from lower left to upper right at about 35 degrees and spans 40% of the image width, with a bright golden-white core, dark dust lanes and bluish outer spiral arms. Its two small satellite galaxies beside it: M32, a compact bright small ellipse just below the core, and M110, a faint fuzzy elongated ellipse just above the disc. Above Andromeda and slightly to the right, clearly separate from its disc, the face-on Triangulum Galaxy (M33): a loose, blue, patchy spiral about one fifth of Andromeda's length. A few tiny faint fuzzy dwarf galaxies scattered far apart. The left third of the image completely empty and black. No foreground stars.

A square 1:1 image. The Milky Way galaxy seen exactly face-on from far above its north pole, a barred spiral: a short bright golden-white central bar, two major spiral arms (Scutum-Centaurus and Perseus) and two fainter minor arms, pink star-forming regions and dark dust lanes along the arms, bluish young stars in the outer arms. The galaxy is centred exactly in the frame and its visible disc spans about 92% of the image width. No stars in the background.

A square 1:1 image. The Sun's neighbourhood seen from far outside, a region about twenty light-years across, almost all of it empty. At the exact centre, a single bright yellow-white star with a soft round glow (the Sun). Left of the centre and a little above it, only 16% of the image width away from the centre, a close pair of bright stars, one yellow-white and one orange, with a much dimmer small red star just beside them (Alpha Centauri A, B and Proxima). No other bright or medium stars anywhere. Behind everything, a deep field of very faint, tiny, distant background stars and a whisper of faint bluish dust, spread evenly out to all four edges.
images.note: Take b. Take a (the first prompt asked for the pair 42% of the way to the left edge) put it 0.266 of the width from the Sun: at the true 4.2 light-years the picture would have been 553 units wide, its starfield ending in a square inside the frame.

images.prompt: A square 1:1 image. A deep field of very faint, tiny, distant stars, spread evenly over the whole image out to all four edges: a few slightly brighter, none bright, with a whisper of faint bluish and brownish dust. No bright stars, no galaxies, no nebulae, no planets, no sun.
images.note: The backdrop of the Solar System and of Earth and the Moon, under their orbits, which stay drawn to scale. It replaced a first take of the Solar System (the Sun in a wide warm haze reaching past Uranus's orbit, which no real dust does).

images.prompt: A square 1:1 image. Use the reference image at the path given below as an exact map: in it, green is land, blue is ocean and black is space, drawn as a globe (an orthographic view centred on 38 degrees north, 100 degrees west). Make a photorealistic image of Earth seen from space with exactly the same framing as the reference: the same globe position and size (its disc 88% of the image width, centred), the same orientation, and every coastline and island exactly where the reference has it, North America in the middle. Natural satellite colours: deep blue oceans, green forests, tan and brown deserts and mountains, white ice on Greenland and the Arctic, a few thin wispy clouds that never hide a coastline, a thin bright blue atmospheric glow at the limb, the whole disc evenly lit. Pure black space around the globe.

A square 1:1 image. The nucleus of a silicon-28 atom seen up close: a tight, roughly spherical cluster of 28 nucleons packed together, centred, the cluster about 72% of the image width. Fourteen protons glow warm red-orange and fourteen neutrons glow cool pale silver-blue, mixed evenly through the cluster so that both colours show all over its surface. Each nucleon is a soft-edged, slightly translucent sphere, as if made of light, so the spheres blend a little where they touch; the cluster's outer edge is hazy, because a nucleus has no hard surface. A faint warm glow around the cluster.

A square 1:1 image. A proton as quantum chromodynamics describes it: a softly glowing, translucent sphere of turbulent violet and magenta energy (the gluon field), centred, filling 84% of the image width. Inside it, three small, intensely bright points of light (quarks) at the corners of a large equilateral triangle centred on the sphere's centre: one at the top, one at the lower right and one at the lower left, each 22% of the image width from the centre. One quark glows red, one green and one blue. Bright, twisting flux tubes of light join the three quarks. The space between them filled with a faint sea of tiny flickering particle pairs and swirling energy.

A square 1:1 image. A single quark, which as far as any experiment can tell is a point with no size: one tiny, intensely bright white point of light at the exact centre of the frame with a small sharp glow, surrounded by a dim, swirling, many-coloured haze (red, green and blue tints) of virtual gluons and fleeting quark-antiquark pairs that is densest near the point and fades out completely by 40% of the image width from the centre. Most of the frame dark.

A square 1:1 image. A single electron, which as far as any experiment can tell is a point with no size: one tiny, intensely bright blue-white point of light at the exact centre of the frame with a small sharp glow, surrounded by a faint, softly flickering cloud of virtual photons and fleeting electron-positron pairs, pale blue and white, densest near the point and fading out completely by 40% of the image width from the centre. Most of the frame dark.

A landscape 4:3 image. Space and time at the Planck length as theories of quantum gravity imagine them: a seething quantum foam of tiny bubbles, wormhole-like handles and warped, rippling fragments of a spacetime grid, iridescent violet, teal and pale gold, dense and turbulent along the bottom of the frame and thinning out to empty black toward the top. Abstract but physical.
